title: I built an experimental Bitcoin futures trading simulator in just over a week with the help of 3 AIs — despite having very limited coding skills
author: Simple-Courage1815
selftext:
Hey everyone!

I want to share a project I've been working on recently: an open-source Android app called \*\*Bitcoin Futures Simulator\*\*.

\*\*GitHub repository:\*\* https://github.com/Joapetis/bitcoin-futuros-android

Before anyone gets too excited, I want to be clear: this is an early-stage experiment, not a profitable trading bot. So far, its simulated trading results have generated more losses than profits. No real money has been involved.

\*\*How it started\*\*

The whole thing began with an old HTML project I had created some time ago and eventually abandoned. The idea behind it never really went away, though.

Recently, I decided to revisit that idea and see how far I could take it with AI assistance. What started as an abandoned project gradually evolved into a functional Android app in a little over a week.

There's a catch: \*\*my programming knowledge is very limited.\*\*

Instead of building everything myself line by line, I've been combining my own ideas, observations, strategy concepts and testing with the coding and debugging capabilities of three different AIs. They've helped generate, modify, review and polish the code throughout the process.

This has become an experiment in its own right. I want to explore not only whether I can turn my ideas into a working application, but also how capable AI systems are at building and improving a relatively complex software project with very little direct human coding.

I'm still the one setting the direction, making decisions, testing results and deciding what should change. The AIs do a substantial part of the coding, but that doesn't mean their output is automatically correct. Bugs, bad assumptions and poor trading results are all part of the process.

\*\*What does the app actually do?\*\*

The current project is an experimental Bitcoin futures paper-trading simulator for Android. Its main components include:

\*\*A multi-timeframe strategy:\*\* primarily focused on 15-minute candles, with 1-hour and 4-hour trend confirmation.

\*\*Trend-following and mean-reversion logic:\*\* different approaches depending on the detected market regime.

\*\*Market microstructure data:\*\* order-book metrics such as spread, imbalance and microprice-related signals.

\*\*Optional on-device AI:\*\* integration with Gemini Nano through Android's AI capabilities when a compatible model and device are available.

\*\*Simulated trading and risk management:\*\* intended to test strategies without risking real funds.

\*\*Continuous experimentation:\*\* the goal is to evaluate what works, identify weaknesses and improve the system over time.

The project is still very much in its infancy. There is plenty to question, test, refactor and improve, and I don't want to present any of its strategies as proven or profitable.

\*\*Why am I sharing it?\*\*

I'd love to turn this into something more collaborative.

If you're a developer, a quantitative trading enthusiast, an Android/Kotlin programmer, someone interested in market microstructure, or simply curious about what AI-assisted development can achieve, I'd genuinely appreciate your input.

You don't need to be an expert in every part of the project. Even identifying bugs, challenging assumptions, improving the architecture, reviewing the trading logic, suggesting better tests or documenting how things work could make a real difference.

My hope is that people can learn from the experiment, contribute their ideas and improvements, and help create something more useful together. In return, contributors get a real-world project to experiment with, review and learn from, while the wider community benefits from any improvements we can make.

I'm especially interested in honest criticism. If you see something fundamentally wrong with the strategy or implementation, I'd rather hear about it than receive empty praise.

\*\*A few important caveats\*\*

This is an experimental project, not financial advice.

All results discussed here are from simulated trading; no real-money trading is involved.

The current simulated performance is negative, so there's a lot of work left to do.

AI-generated code can contain bugs and needs independent review and testing.

The app is not ready to be treated as a reliable or profitable trading system.

If you'd like to explore the code, suggest an improvement, open an issue or contribute, you're welcome to check out the repository.

I'd love to hear your thoughts. Thanks for reading!

comments.author: leroylabs
comments.body: The first thing I’d test is whether the order-book features and candle logic share a valid clock. Spread, imbalance, and microprice can change many times inside a 15-minute candle, so replaying them from a snapshot near the close could leak information or assume an impossible fill. Save timestamped book updates, the exact decision time, and the next executable bid/ask, then compare results with those features removed. I’d also keep Gemini Nano advisory-only until its output is deterministic enough to replay across compatible devices. The image only shows the GitHub card with 1 contributor and no issues, stars, or forks, not performance evidence.

replies.author: Simple-Courage1815
replies.body:
Sorry, this is my first time using GitHub. I'll try to update the information in more detail when I have some time.
What I can tell you is that there's a bug in the learning process that I haven't been able to fix yet, as well as another issue with capital management.
I'm still very much a beginner, and I'm trying to recover the results from my initial tests. Back then, it generated two trades with a 73% profit before closing, with a 43% profit after deducting fees.

comments.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
comments.body: Saying plainly that the simulated results are negative makes this a good project to review. Two things I'd look at first in the code: that every decision uses only closed candles and data available at that time (the multi-timeframe confirmation is a common place for a 1-hour or 4-hour bar that hasn't closed yet to sneak in), and that the order-book signals are tested with realistic delay, since microprice and imbalance usually fade within seconds. A simple baseline helps too: run the same simulator with random entries and identical exits, so you can see whether any of the three strategy layers beats that. Cymetica's Backtest Labs is one place to see how rule changes get compared against a benchmark.

comments.author: QuanTradin
comments.body: saying up front that the sim loses more than it makes is the most useful line in the post. one thing to check: does it charge funding and taker fees on every fill? on perps those two alone can turn a flat strategy into a steady bleed.

replies.author: Simple-Courage1815
replies.body:
In theory, that’s already implemented in the bot. I’m not sure whether it’s been implemented correctly, though. At least in one of the early versions, it worked really well and calculated everything accurately, taking the exchange fees into account.

At this point, after tweaking things and changing a few values here and there, I’m not sure if it’s still working properly.

I ran into a major issue with saving the learning data. I had already simulated over 1,200 trades, achieved a 63% win rate, and made a 73% profit across two trades, which ended up at 43% net profit after accounting for fees. The learning data was wiped, and I’m not sure whether it was caused by a change in the way it was saved or by an attempt to include more parameters in the saved data.

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: that drift after tweaking is really common. cheapest check I know: take one closed trade, work out the fee and funding by hand from the exchange's own fee page, and compare it to what the sim booked. if the two differ, every result after that carries the same leak.

comments.author: stratcore
comments.body:
I found one specific restart check in your published LearningBrain.kt (file commit 4766cc1). toJson() saves the target, but load() raises it to at least 0.0045. Your aggressive mode sets 0.0042. A saved 0.42% target therefore comes back as 0.45%, a 3-basis-point change, even before another trade.



That matters when comparing versions: a restart can change the strategy being measured. Save a version-5 state, load it into a fresh instance, and compare target, stop, sample counts and weights before feeding both instances the same recorded inputs. The unchanged-version case should preserve the intended settings; an intentional migration should have its own expected values.



This source-level finding does not establish why the 1,200 trades disappeared. Keep an untouched backup while checking that separately. Reply "sheet" if you'd like the free restart-test rule sheet here in the thread.
